subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview:
Welcome to Unit 17! In this unit you will become confident at multiplying and dividing larger numbers using efficient written methods. You already know your multiplication facts and you can multiply and divide small numbers in your head. Now you will learn how to handle 2-digit and 3-digit numbers by a 1-digit number quickly and accurately, using the column method for multiplication and an efficient method for division.

This unit is built for self-paced learning. That means you move at your own speed. Read each explanation slowly, copy every worked example onto paper and work it through yourself, and only move on when the steps feel clear. Your AI tutor is available day and night to set you extra practice, explain a step in a fresh way, or mark your working. Your teacher will also meet with you about twice a week to help with anything that feels tricky.

Keep a pencil and plenty of paper beside you as you read. Multiplication and division are not spectator sports – you must do them, digit by digit, to truly learn them. Write the numbers neatly in columns, line up the place value carefully, and say each step out loud. If you make a mistake, that is not a failure; it simply shows you exactly which step to practise next. Every skill in this unit rests on care and neatness, so slow, tidy work will serve you far better than rushing.

outcomes: Use an efficient column method to multiply 2-digit and 3-digit numbers by a 1-digit number.
Use an efficient written method for division, including dividing with remainders.
Estimate products and quotients to check that your answers are reasonable.
Interpret remainders correctly in different real-world situations.
Solve word problems that involve multiplication and division.
Explain the relationship between multiplication and division, and use one to check the other.
Apply multiplication and division to multi-step problems.
Create and solve your own word problems for a given calculation.

concepts.title: The Column Method for Multiplication
concepts.explanation:
Multiplication is a fast way of adding equal groups. If Halima has 5 baskets with 3 mangoes in each, she has 5 × 3 = 15 mangoes. The numbers being multiplied are called factors, and the answer is called the product. In 7 × 8 = 56, the factors are 7 and 8 and the product is 56.

For small numbers you can use facts you already know. But when the numbers get larger – say 346 × 9 – you need an efficient written method. The column method lines the digits up by place value and multiplies one column at a time, working from right to left (ones first, then tens, then hundreds). Whenever a column gives more than 9, you write the ones digit down and carry the tens to the next column, just as you do in column addition.

Let us work through 346 × 9 together, one careful step at a time.

Step 1 – Set it out. Write the larger number on top and the 1-digit number underneath, lining up the ones. Draw a line beneath.

Step 2 – Estimate first. Round 346 to 350 and think 350 × 9, or even 350 × 10 = 3,500. So the answer should be somewhere near 3,000–3,500. Keeping this estimate in mind protects you from a silly slip.

Step 3 – Multiply the ones. 6 × 9 = 54. Write the 4 in the ones column and carry the 5 into the tens column.

Step 4 – Multiply the tens. 4 × 9 = 36, then add the carried 5 to get 41. Write the 1 in the tens column and carry the 4 into the hundreds column.

Step 5 – Multiply the hundreds. 3 × 9 = 27, then add the carried 4 to get 31. There are no more columns, so write 31 in full. Reading down, the answer is 3,114.
concepts.example: Step 6 – Check against the estimate. Our answer 3,114 is close to our estimate of 3,500, so it is reasonable. If we had got 384 or 31,140 we would know at once that something had gone wrong.

concepts.title: Estimating Products and Multiplying with Zeros
concepts.explanation:
Estimating before you calculate is a habit that good mathematicians keep for life. An estimate is a quick, rough answer using rounded numbers. It is not the real answer – it is a guard that warns you if your real answer is far too big or far too small.

To estimate a product: round each number to something easy, multiply the rounded numbers, then compare. For example, to estimate 78 × 6, round 78 up to 80. Then 80 × 6 = 480, so 78 × 6 should be a little under 480 (because we rounded 78 up). The exact answer is 468 – nicely close. To estimate 287 × 6, round 287 to 300: 300 × 6 = 1,800, so expect an answer a bit below 1,800. The exact answer is 1,722.

Multiplying with zeros uses exactly the same column method, but you must be careful with place value. Take 205 × 4. Working right to left: 5 × 4 = 20, so write 0 and carry 2. Then the middle digit: 0 × 4 = 0, and adding the carried 2 gives 2. Finally 2 × 4 = 8. The answer is 820. The zero in 205 does not disappear – it holds the tens place so the digits stay in their correct columns. A common slip is to skip a zero column and squash the digits together; going column by column, and never missing one, keeps you safe.

Here is a useful thinking tip. Rounding up gives an estimate that is a little too big, and rounding down gives one that is a little too small. Knowing which way you rounded tells you whether the true answer should sit just below or just above your estimate, which makes your check even sharper.
concepts.example: Estimating is also a real-world skill that traders use every day. When Ibrahim sells 7 sacks of maize at 495 shillings each, he does not need the exact total to know roughly how much money to expect – he rounds 495 to 500 and thinks 500 × 7 = 3,500 shillings. Later he works out the exact figure, 3,465 shillings, and because it sits just below his estimate (he rounded up), he knows it is right. Practising estimation this way trains your number sense so that a wrong answer will feel wrong straight away, even before you check it carefully.

concepts.title: An Efficient Method for Division
concepts.explanation:
Division is sharing or grouping equally. There are two ways to picture it. Sharing: 15 ÷ 3 can mean sharing 15 dates equally among 3 children, giving 5 each. Grouping: 15 ÷ 3 can also mean making groups of 3 from 15 dates, giving 5 groups. Both give the same answer, 5.

Division has its own special words. The number you are dividing is the dividend. The number you divide by is the divisor. The answer is the quotient, and anything left over is the remainder. In 17 ÷ 4 = 4 remainder 1, the 17 is the dividend, the 4 you divide by is the divisor, the 4 in the answer is the quotient, and the 1 left over is the remainder.

For larger numbers we use an efficient written method often called short division, working from the left (the biggest place) towards the right. Let us divide 75 ÷ 4 step by step.

Step 1 – Estimate. 80 ÷ 4 = 20, so the answer should be near 20.

Step 2 – Divide the tens. How many 4s in 7 (the 7 tens)? 7 ÷ 4 = 1 remainder 3. Write 1 in the tens place of the answer, and carry the remainder of 3 tens across to the ones, making the 5 ones into 35.

Step 3 – Divide the ones. How many 4s in 35? 35 ÷ 4 = 8 remainder 3. Write 8 in the ones place of the answer, and 3 is left over.

Step 4 – Read the answer. 75 ÷ 4 = 18 remainder 3, which is close to our estimate of 20.
concepts.example: The same method works for 3-digit numbers. For 372 ÷ 4 you divide the hundreds first (3 ÷ 4 = 0 remainder 3, so carry 3 hundreds to make 37 tens), then the tens (37 ÷ 4 = 9 remainder 1, carry 1 ten to make 12 ones), then the ones (12 ÷ 4 = 3). The answer is 93. Always work left to right, carrying each remainder to the next column.

concepts.title: Interpreting Remainders
concepts.explanation:
A remainder is the amount left over when a number does not divide exactly. The clever part is deciding what to do with it, because that depends entirely on the story of the problem. There are four common ways to handle a remainder.

1. Leave it as a whole number. If 25 children are put into teams of 4, then 25 ÷ 4 = 6 remainder 1, so you make 6 teams with 1 child left over. The remainder simply tells you how many are not in a full team.

2. Round up. If you need at least 50 pencils and they come in packs of 6, then 50 ÷ 6 = 8 remainder 2. Eight packs give only 48, which is not enough, so you must buy 9 packs. When you need enough to cover everyone, you round up.

3. Round down (ignore it). If 23 stickers are shared 4 to a child, then 23 ÷ 4 = 5 remainder 3, so 5 children get a full set and the 3 spare stickers are not enough for another full set. When you can only count complete groups, you round down.

4. Express it as a fraction. If 7 flatbreads (anjero) are shared equally among 3 people, then 7 ÷ 3 = 2 remainder 1, and that last one is split three ways: each person gets 2 and one-third. When something can be cut up and shared, the remainder becomes a fraction.
concepts.example: So the very same calculation can give different sensible answers depending on the question. Always ask yourself: does the story want whole leftovers, enough to cover everyone, only complete groups, or a fair share of the last piece? Reading the question carefully is just as important as the dividing itself.

concepts.title: Multiplication and Division Are Linked
concepts.explanation:
Multiplication and division are inverse operations – each one undoes the other. Because 8 × 6 = 48, we also know 48 ÷ 6 = 8 and 48 ÷ 8 = 6. These four facts form a fact family. Knowing this link is powerful, because it lets you check a division by multiplying, and check a multiplication by dividing.

To check a division, multiply the quotient by the divisor and add the remainder; you should get back the dividend. For example, check 75 ÷ 4 = 18 remainder 3: multiply 18 × 4 = 72, then add the remainder 72 + 3 = 75. Since 75 equals the number we started with, the answer is correct. This simple check will catch most mistakes, so make it a habit after every division.

The inverse link also helps with missing-number problems. If □ × 7 = 56, you can find the missing factor by dividing: 56 ÷ 7 = 8, so □ = 8. If 81 ÷ □ = 9, you can rearrange to □ × 9 = 81, so □ = 81 ÷ 9 = 9. Whenever a number is hidden, ask whether multiplying or dividing the numbers you can see will reveal it.
concepts.example: This relationship explains something you may already have noticed: the highest remainder you can ever get when dividing by a number is one less than that number. When you divide by 4, the remainder can only be 0, 1, 2 or 3, because a remainder of 4 would make another whole group. When you divide by 7, the largest possible remainder is 6. This is a direct result of what division means, and it gives you a quick way to check a division has not gone wrong: if your remainder is ever equal to or larger than the divisor, you have made a mistake and should divide once more.

concepts.title: Choosing the Right Operation in Word Problems
concepts.explanation:
The hardest part of a word problem is often deciding whether to multiply or divide. Here is a reliable guide.

Multiply when you know the number of groups and how many are in each group, and you want the total. You are combining equal groups. Watch for words like each, every, per, at and times. Example: 28 boxes with 12 pencils in each box – multiply to find the total.

Divide when you know the total and either the number of groups or the size of each group, and you want to find the other. You are sharing equally or making equal groups. Watch for words like share, split equally, each, per and how many groups. Example: 96 rolls put into bags of 8 – divide to find how many bags.

A dependable seven-step routine works for almost any word problem: Read the problem carefully; Identify the important numbers; Decide on multiply or divide; Estimate the answer; Calculate with an efficient method; Check it is reasonable and interpret any remainder; then Answer in a full sentence that matches the question. Following these steps every time turns a confusing paragraph into a clear plan.

Some problems need more than one step. For example: a school buys 15 boxes of 24 pencils, then has 72 left over – how many were used? First multiply to find the total, 15 × 24 = 360, then subtract the leftover, 360 − 72 = 288 used. In multi-step problems, do one operation at a time and write down each result so you never lose your place.

You have now met six big ideas: the column method for multiplication, estimating and multiplying with zeros, an efficient method for division, interpreting remainders, the inverse link between multiplication and division, and choosing the right operation in word problems. These ideas are not separate – they work as a team. When Idris buys sacks of grain at the Mogadishu market, he multiplies to find the cost and estimates first to be sure the total looks right. When Khadija packs 237 apples into crates of 6, she divides, then thinks carefully about the 3 apples left over.
concepts.example: The best way to lock these skills into your memory is to use them with real numbers around your home and neighbourhood. Work out the cost of several items at the same price. Share a bowl of dates fairly and notice the remainder. Estimate an answer before you calculate, then check your division by multiplying back. Every time you do this, your number sense grows stronger, and the harder maths in later units – long multiplication, long division, fractions and ratio – will feel much easier. Now let us practise together with some fully worked examples.

methods.title: How to multiply a 2- or 3-digit number by a 1-digit number
steps: Write the larger number on top, the 1-digit number below, lining up the ones.
Estimate the answer by rounding.
Multiply the ones; write the ones digit and carry the rest.
Multiply the tens, add the carried digit; write and carry.
Multiply the hundreds, add the carried digit; write the result.
Compare with your estimate to check it is reasonable.

methods.title: How to divide using short division
steps: Estimate the answer by rounding.
Divide the highest place value first.
Carry any remainder across to the next digit.
Continue until every digit is divided.
Write the quotient and any final remainder, then check by multiplying.

methods.title: How to interpret a remainder
steps: Read the story to see what the remainder means.
Leave it whole, round up, round down, or write it as a fraction — whichever fits.
Answer the question in a full sentence.

methods.title: Divide with a remainder
steps: Estimate: 60 ÷ 6 = 10.
Tens: 6 ÷ 6 = 1, no remainder, write 1.
Ones: 8 ÷ 6 = 1 remainder 2, write 1.
Answer: 11 remainder 2.

methods.title: Divide a 3-digit number
steps: Hundreds: 4 ÷ 9 = 0 remainder 4, carry 4 to make 43 tens.
Tens: 43 ÷ 9 = 4 remainder 7, write 4, carry 7 to make 78 ones.
Ones: 78 ÷ 9 = 8 remainder 6, write 8.
Answer: 48 remainder 6.

methods.title: Interpret a remainder (round up)
methods.example: A bus holds 36 children. 145 children go on a trip. How many buses are needed?
steps: 145 ÷ 36: four buses carry 4 × 36 = 144, leaving 1 child.
That last child still needs a seat, so round up to 5 buses.
Here the remainder means we need one more bus.

workedExamples.title: Multiply a 2-digit number
workedExamples.solution: Estimate first: 80 × 6 = 480. Ones: 8 × 6 = 48, write 8, carry 4. Tens: 7 × 6 = 42, add the carried 4 to get 46, write 46. Answer: 468, close to the estimate of 480.

workedExamples.title: Multiply a 3-digit number
workedExamples.solution: Estimate: 500 × 7 = 3,500. Ones: 2 × 7 = 14, write 4, carry 1. Tens: 6 × 7 = 42, add 1 to get 43, write 3, carry 4. Hundreds: 4 × 7 = 28, add 4 to get 32, write 32. Answer: 3,234, near the estimate.

workedExamples.title: Multiply with a zero
workedExamples.solution: Ones: 3 × 7 = 21, write 1, carry 2. Tens: 0 × 7 = 0, add the carried 2 to get 2, write 2. Hundreds: 5 × 7 = 35, write 35. Answer: 3,521. The middle zero still needs its own column.

workedExamples.title: Divide with a remainder
workedExamples.solution: Estimate: 60 ÷ 6 = 10. Tens: 6 ÷ 6 = 1, no remainder, write 1. Ones: 8 ÷ 6 = 1 remainder 2, write 1. Answer: 11 remainder 2. Check: 11 × 6 = 66, and 66 + 2 = 68. Correct.

workedExamples.title: Divide a 3-digit number
workedExamples.solution: Hundreds: 4 ÷ 9 = 0 remainder 4, carry 4 to make 43 tens. Tens: 43 ÷ 9 = 4 remainder 7, write 4, carry 7 to make 78 ones. Ones: 78 ÷ 9 = 8 remainder 6, write 8. Answer: 48 remainder 6. Check: 48 × 9 = 432, and 432 + 6 = 438. Correct.

workedExamples.title: Interpret a remainder (round up)
workedExamples.prompt: A bus holds 36 children. 145 children go on a trip. How many buses are needed?
workedExamples.solution: 145 ÷ 36: four buses carry 4 × 36 = 144, leaving 1 child. That last child still needs a seat, so round up to 5 buses. Here the remainder means we need one more bus.

workedExamples.title: A multiplication word problem
workedExamples.prompt: A cinema has 28 rows with 6 seats in each row. How many seats are there in total?
workedExamples.solution: Equal groups, so multiply: 28 × 6. Ones: 8 × 6 = 48, write 8, carry 4. Tens: 2 × 6 = 12, add 4 to get 16, write 16. Answer: 168 seats.

workedExamples.title: A two-step problem
workedExamples.prompt: Hassan has 8 fields and plants 45 trees in each. A storm damages 27 trees. How many healthy trees remain?
workedExamples.solution: Step 1, total trees: 8 × 45 = 360. Step 2, subtract the damaged trees: 360 − 27 = 333 healthy trees. Doing one step at a time keeps the working clear.

workedExamples.title: A missing-number problem
workedExamples.solution: Use the inverse link. If 96 ÷ □ = 12, then □ × 12 = 96, so □ = 96 ÷ 12 = 8. Check: 96 ÷ 8 = 12. Whenever a number is hidden, look for a multiplication or division that reveals it.

workedExamples.title: A remainder as a fraction
workedExamples.prompt: Seven mangoes are shared equally among 3 children. How many does each child get?
workedExamples.solution: 7 ÷ 3 = 2 remainder 1. The single mango left over is split three ways, giving each child one-third more. So each child gets 2 and one-third mangoes. Because a mango can be cut up, the remainder becomes a fraction rather than being left whole.

workedExamples.title: Find the missing number
workedExamples.prompt: Find the missing number: a) □ × 7 = 56 b) 81 ÷ □ = 9.

workedExamples.title: Find the missing digits
workedExamples.prompt: Find the missing digits: a) 2□5 ÷ 5 = 43 b) 3□ × 4 = 124.
workedExamples.solution: a) 215 ÷ 5 = 43, missing digit 1; b) 31 × 4 = 124, missing digit 1.

activities.title: Market Stall Multiplication
activities.materials: small stones or bottle caps as pretend shillings, paper price labels.
steps: Set up a pretend market stall with items priced at the same amount, for example mangoes at 7 shillings each.
Choose how many of one item a customer buys, such as 8 mangoes.
Work out the total cost with the column method, estimating first.
Pay with your stones and check the total is right. Swap roles and try new prices.
This activity shows how multiplication finds the total cost of equal-priced items every day at the market.

activities.title: Sharing Dates (Division and Remainders)
activities.materials: a handful of dates, beans or stones, and a few small bowls.
steps: Count out a number of dates, for example 43, and choose a number of bowls, for example 5.
Share the dates equally, one at a time, into the bowls.
Count how many are in each bowl and how many are left over – that leftover is the remainder.
Write the division: 43 ÷ 5 = 8 remainder 3. Try again with different numbers and predict the remainder first.

activities.title: Fact Family Triangles
steps: Draw a large triangle and write a product at the top corner, for example 48.
Write its two factors, 6 and 8, in the bottom corners.
Write all four facts in the family: 6 × 8 = 48, 8 × 6 = 48, 48 ÷ 6 = 8, 48 ÷ 8 = 6.
Make five more triangles and see how quickly you can write each fact family.
Fact families show clearly how multiplication and division are linked as inverse operations.

activities.title: Remainder Investigation
activities.materials: paper, a pencil, and a small pile of counters.
steps: Choose a divisor, for example 4.
Divide the numbers 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15 and 16 by 4 and record each remainder.
Look at the pattern of remainders: 2, 3, 0, 1, 2, 3, 0. What do you notice?
Predict: what is the largest remainder possible when dividing by 4? By 7? Check with counters.
You should discover that the remainder is always smaller than the divisor – a very useful rule.

activities.title: Estimation Challenge (Family Game)
activities.materials: your family or a friend, paper and a pencil.
steps: One player writes a multiplication such as 287 × 6 or a division such as 438 ÷ 9.
Everyone quickly writes an estimate by rounding, before any exact working.
Now calculate the exact answer with a written method.
The player whose estimate is closest to the exact answer wins the round. Play several rounds.

activities.title: Design Your Own Word Problem
steps: Pick a calculation, for example 8 × 42 = 336 or 216 ÷ 6 = 36.
Choose a real context you know: livestock, market shopping, water collection, or a football match.
Write a clear word problem whose answer is your chosen calculation.
Give your problem to a family member or classmate to solve, then check their working together.

After your activities, talk or write about: Which activity helped you understand remainders best? What was the trickiest part of the column method? Which do you find easier, multiplication or division, and why? Share your answers with your teacher at your next session.

rules.title: Column Multiplication Rule
rules.text: Line up place value and work from right to left: ones, then tens, then hundreds. If a column gives more than 9, write the ones digit and carry the tens to the next column. Add any carried digit before you write the next column.

rules.title: Division Rule
rules.text: Work from left to right: divide the biggest place first. Carry each remainder across to the next column. The remainder is always smaller than the divisor.

rules.title: Estimate and Check Rule
rules.text: Estimate first by rounding, so you can spot a silly answer. Check a division by multiplying the quotient by the divisor and adding the remainder.

commonMistakes: Add the carry before writing that column
Give the zero its own multiply step
Round up to cover everyone; down for full groups
Groups and total known → multiply; total known → divide

reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 399 × 6 = 2,394, which is very close to 2,400, so it is a good estimate.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Ahmed says: multiply a number by 6 then divide by 3, and it is the same as multiplying by 2. Is he correct? Explain.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Yes – multiplying by 6 then dividing by 3 is the same as multiplying by 6 ÷ 3 = 2; for example 5 × 6 = 30, 30 ÷ 3 = 10, and 5 × 2 = 10.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Find a 2-digit number that gives a remainder of 3 when divided by 4 and a remainder of 2 when divided by 5.
What is the smallest 3-digit number that is divisible by both 6 and 8?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 120 — the lowest common multiple of 6 and 8 is 24, and the smallest 3-digit multiple of 24 is 24 × 5 = 120.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Choosing the Right Operation in Word Problems.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The hardest part of a word problem is often deciding whether to multiply or divide. Here is a reliable guide. Multiply when you know the number of groups and how many are in each group, and you want the total. You are combining equal groups. Watch for words like each, every, per, at and times. Example: 28 boxes with 12 pencils in each box – multiply to find the total.
